content: Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) utilize peptides derived from proteins that are almost exclusively produced by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other mycobacteria within the M. tuberculosis complex. These proteins are absent in Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccines and most non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Blood is collected in specialized tubes coated with these TB-specific antigenic peptides and incubated. In individuals infected with TB, interferon-gamma is released when their blood is exposed to these antigens, whereas this response is absent in uninfected individuals. IGRAs offer several advantages, including requiring only a single visit, providing results within 24 hours, and avoiding false-positive results due to prior BCG vaccination. However, disadvantages include higher costs, the need for phlebotomy, rapid processing of blood samples, laboratory infrastructure, and reduced accuracy in individuals living with HIV. In practice, the choice between IGRAs and the tuberculin skin test (TST) often depends on test availability and affordability. TST may require fewer resources and is more familiar to practitioners in resource-limited settings, but global shortages of tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) have limited its use in scaling up TB preventive treatment (TPT) programs. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends several TPT regimens for children and adolescents with drug-susceptible TB. These include six or nine months of daily isoniazid (6H or 9H) for all ages, three months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP) for those aged two years and older, three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin (3HR) for all ages, one month of daily isoniazid plus rifapentine (1HP) for those aged 13 years and older, and four months of daily rifampicin (4R) for all ages. While 4R is an option, it lacks a suitable pediatric formulation and is therefore not widely included. Historically, the term isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) was used when 6H was the primary regimen, but with the availability of alternative regimens, TB preventive treatment (TPT) is now preferred. Young children under five years of age are particularly vulnerable to TB due to their higher risk of disease progression and severe forms such as TB meningitis or disseminated TB. Diagnosing TB in this age group is challenging due to the paucibacillary nature of the disease. Preventing pediatric TB through TPT is therefore critical. Among children, the 3HR regimen is better tolerated, shorter, and more child-friendly than 6H or 9H, as dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations are available. A study in four African countries demonstrated high uptake, completion rates, and low rates of mild adverse events with 3HR. In the absence of appropriate rifapentine dosages for younger children, national programs may consider scaling up 3HR for all ages. Children weighing under 25 kg, including those under two years, can use the same FDC formulation as the continuation phase of TB treatment. Those weighing over 25 kg may receive 3HP (if available for adults) or 3HR using adult FDCs of rifampicin and isoniazid. For children living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens such as lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), dolutegravir (DTG), or nevirapine (NVP), the 6H regimen remains the most suitable option due to ongoing pharmacokinetic and safety studies on rifapentine-based TPT regimens in this population. Close monitoring for isoniazid-induced hepatitis is necessary, especially given potential drug-drug interactions. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplementation is recommended for individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, such as those with malnutrition, HIV, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Exclusively breastfed infants on isoniazid should also receive vitamin B6 supplementation. For household contacts of individuals with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or isoniazid monoresistance, the risk of TB infection is higher than for contacts of drug-susceptible TB cases. WHO suggests using levofloxacin for six months, along with other TB medicines such as ethambutol or ethionamide (if tolerated), for child contacts of MDR-TB cases. Regardless of treatment, clinical follow-up for two years is recommended, with active investigation of any emergent TB symptoms and initiation of treatment as needed. Adherence to TPT is influenced by various factors, including personal motivation, beliefs about health, perceived risks and benefits, comorbidities, family environment, and the complexity or toxicity of the treatment regimen. Strategies to promote adherence include ensuring confidentiality, providing clear information about TPT options and duration, involving family members in health education, and addressing barriers such as stigma, transportation costs, or caregiver illness. For children, the availability of child-friendly formulations and clear instructions for caregivers on medication administration are essential. Adolescents living with HIV may require direct education and adherence support. Shorter TPT regimens, such as 3HP or 1HP, are associated with better adherence and higher treatment completion rates. If treatment interruptions occur, the next steps depend on the duration of the interruption and the proportion of doses completed. For example, if less than 80% of doses are taken and the treatment course cannot be completed within the expected timeframe, restarting the full TPT course may be necessary.g., triage, respiratory separation, and prompt initiation of effective TB treatment), environmental controls (e.g., ventilation systems and ultraviolet germicidal irradiation), and respiratory protection (e.g., particulate respirators). Adolescents aged 10–19 years pose a similar transmission risk as adults, while children under 10 years are less likely to transmit TB. However, poor IPC practices can still facilitate transmission from adults or adolescents to children. In summary, effective TB prevention in children and adolescents requires a combination of appropriate TPT regimens, adherence support, and robust IPC practices.
